name: Drivacet
description: Drivacet is a synthetic dopaminergic drive enhancer that targets motivational circuitry specifically — the wanting system rather than the reward system — producing a sustained, intense sense of purpose and drive toward goal-directed behavior. Unlike stimulants, it does not accelerate cognition or cause euphoria; it simply makes the user feel that what they are currently doing is urgently, profoundly worth doing. It is marketed to productivity-focused professionals but is widely used on the Shelf by people who need to get through things they would otherwise find impossible to face.
effects: Intense, focused motivational drive toward current tasks
Elimination of procrastination and task-initiation difficulty
Sense of purpose and urgency without anxiety
Sustained engagement with repetitive or unpleasant work
side_effects: Motivation is non-selective — users feel driven toward whatever they are doing, not necessarily what they should be doing
Anhedonia between doses as the brain's drive system recalibrates
Compulsive redosing common — the absence of drive feels unbearable after prolonged use
Blunting of natural rest signals — users push through exhaustion and injury
Long-term use associated with burnout syndrome that is resistant to conventional treatment
Can be weaponized — dosing someone before directing them toward a desired task
cultural_context: Drivacet is the drug that makes GLMZ run. It is why the Shelf keeps producing, why Tier 2 workers pull double shifts, why Tier 3 professionals hit their KPIs. It is also deeply exploitative — it does not create capacity, it borrows from the future. Heavy users describe the eventual crash not as tiredness but as a complete inability to want anything at all. Helix markets it as empowerment. Critics call it 'the whip you hold yourself.'
story_hooks: A Shelf labor organizer realizes that the factory floor's 90% Drivacet usage rate is not coincidental — the company has been adding a Drivacet analog to the filtered air in the production zone, and workers are technically dosed without consent every shift

A Helix researcher who helped develop Drivacet has spent the last two years unable to feel motivated to do anything — the irony is not lost on them, but neither is the fact that they know too much to be allowed to quit quietly
A Tier 3 professional realizes they have been on Drivacet so long they have no idea what they actually want, separate from what they have been driven to pursue — and begins trying to find out
